analysis.one_liner: Requires social media, gaming, and streaming platforms to protect minors online, with parental controls, defaults, audits, and enforcement.
analysis.headline: The bill had 72 Senate cosponsors — 36 Republicans, 35 Democrats, 1 Independent — and cleared committee without a recorded dissent, but it never received a vote in either chamber before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required online platforms that minors are likely to use to design products that prevent harms like bullying, sexual exploitation, and addiction-like use. It would have given minors and parents settings to limit contact, data sharing, algorithmic recommendations, and screen time, turned the most protective settings on by default for children, barred targeted advertising to minors, and required large platforms to publish annual risk reports based on independent audits. Enforcement would have run through the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general.
analysis.who_benefits: Minors under 17 and their parents: the bill would have required platforms to provide easy-to-use safeguards (limits on who can contact a child, controls on recommendation algorithms and time spent, geolocation restrictions) with the most protective settings enabled by default for children under 13 [S4]. It would have banned facilitating ads for drugs, tobacco, gambling, and alcohol to minors, required disclosure of why a child is being targeted by an ad, and given users a version of large platforms' feeds that does not prioritize content based on personal data [S3][S4]. It would also have created a program giving university and nonprofit researchers access to platform data to study harms to minors, and given the FTC and state attorneys general power to sue violators [S2][S4].

how_it_helps.text: Platforms must take reasonable design measures to prevent and mitigate harms to minors, including anxiety, depression, eating disorders, addiction-like usage patterns, bullying, sexual exploitation, and marketing of drugs, tobacco, gambling, or alcohol.

Minors get safeguards — limits on who can contact them, controls over recommendation systems including a chronological-feed option, time limits, and account deletion — and for children under 13 the most protective settings and parental tools must be on by default.
Platforms must give parents tools to view and control a child's privacy settings, restrict purchases, and monitor time spent, with clear notice to the child when those tools are applied.

Large platforms (over 10 million monthly U.S. users) must publish annual public reports on risks of harm to minors based on an independent third-party audit, including an accounting of minors' time on the platform and how recommendation and ad systems contribute to harms.

The reported version adds 'filter bubble' requirements: large websites and apps must notify users that they use personalized recommendation algorithms and offer a version that does not prioritize content based on user-specific data.
University and nonprofit researchers would gain a program to access platform data sets to study harms to minors, and the FTC and state attorneys general could enforce the law in court.

analysis.who_pays: Large social media, video game, and streaming companies, which would bear the cost of redesigning products, running independent audits, building parental-control systems, limiting ad targeting to minors, and providing data to researchers — plus reduced engagement and ad revenue from young users if the changes curb compulsive use.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large social media, gaming, and ad businesses

drawbacks.text: The core 'duty of care' lists broad harm categories such as anxiety, depression, and addiction-like usage without specifying what design measures satisfy them, leaving platforms, the FTC, and courts to sort out compliance — which could push platforms toward over-restricting content for minors rather than risk liability.

The bill relies on platforms applying rules to users they 'know' are minors, but it does not require platforms to build age-verification systems and only commissions a study of how device-level age verification might work, so coverage of teens who misstate their age is uncertain.

The reported version's filter-bubble provisions reach beyond children, requiring large websites and search engines generally to provide notice of algorithmic feeds and a non-personalized version — a burden its opponents characterized as regulating how all users see content.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's concrete protections — protective defaults for children, parental tools, an opt-out from engagement-driven feeds, an ad-targeting ban for minors, mandatory audits, and independent research access — address documented worries from many parents about social media's effects on kids. The honest costs are compliance burdens on platforms, a broad duty of care that could be enforced unevenly or lead to over-blocking of legitimate content for teens, and the fact that age coverage is uncertain because platforms are not required to verify ages. Weighing those, it was a substantive, if imperfect, consumer-protection bill rather than a badly designed one.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee approved it unanimously and it was placed on the Senate's calendar of business in December 2023, but no Senate leader ever brought it to the floor for a vote, the House never considered it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in May 2023 with bipartisan sponsorship led by Senator Blumenthal and Senator Blackburn and was referred to the Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee.
In July 2023 the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.
On December 13, 2023 the committee, chaired by Senator Cantwell, formally reported the bill with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 287) on December 13, 2023 — meaning it was eligible for a floor vote — but no further action followed.
By the time the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, the bill had never received a vote in the Senate or the House, and all bills not passed by then die and must be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large social media, gaming, and streaming companies are better off: they avoided the bill's design mandates, mandatory independent audits, researcher access to their data, targeted-advertising restrictions on minors, and FTC and state attorney general enforcement. The public got none of the protections the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large social media and gaming platforms

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Kids Online Safety Act and organized a large bipartisan cosponsor list.

for.name: Sen. Marsha Blackburn
for.what_they_did: Joined as a lead Republican sponsor, making the bill a bipartisan effort from introduction.

for.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
for.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
for.what_they_did: Her committee reported the bill favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute in December 2023.

for.name: 72 Senate cosponsors (36 R, 35 D, 1 I)
for.role: More than two-thirds of the Senate
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill one of the largest bipartisan rosters of the Congress.

for.name: Senate Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Voted in July 2023 to order the bill reported favorably with an amendment.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.role: Majority party leadership controlling the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote despite its placement on the calendar and overwhelming cosponsorship.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Speaker and House leadership controlling the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the Kids Online Safety Act to the House floor; the House took no action on the bill in the entire Congress.

against.name: Major social media platforms and their trade groups
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against the bill and warned its duty-of-care language could force censorship of content for minors.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split almost evenly — 36 Republicans, 35 Democrats, and 1 Independent — and the Commerce Committee reported the bill favorably with no recorded opposition [S5][S6].

industries.note: The bill would have imposed a duty of care, protective default settings, parental tools, annual audited risk reports, and access to their data for independent researchers, with FTC and state attorney general enforcement. Their business depends on engagement from young users, which the bill was designed to curb.

Platforms would have been barred from facilitating ads for drugs, tobacco, gambling, and alcohol to minors and would have had to disclose why an ad was directed at a specific child and how their data was used — cutting into the personalized ad targeting aimed at young users.

industries.industry: Online video game and streaming services
industries.note: Games with user communication or in-game purchases and video streaming services are covered platforms under the bill, so they would have faced the same safeguards, default settings, and parental-control requirements.

industries.industry: Broadband providers, email, videoconferencing, and direct messaging services
industries.note: These services are explicitly exempt from the bill's requirements, leaving their competitors in social media to bear the compliance costs.
